children: By Janet H. Cho
Audiences can't get enough of movies that scare them out of their seats.

This weekend, Other Mommy, Universal Pictures' horror movie about a sinister entity that emerges from an 8-year-old girl's closet to threaten her and her family, topped the weekend box office with an estimated $27.5 million in ticket sales its North American debut, or nearly a third of the weekend's estimated $85.2 million.
Other Mommy, starring Jessica Chastain and Arabella Olivia Clark, sold another $17.7 million internationally for a total of $45.2 million worldwide.

Horror is one of the biggest box office stories of the year, according to Rentrak's head of marketplace trends Paul Dergarabedian. "Other Mommy marks the sixth horror or horror-comedy film to open at No. one domestically this year," he noted, with Send Help, Scream 7, Backrooms, Scary Movie, and Resident Evil rounding out the list.

The year to date domestic box office sales through Sunday is at an estimated $8.07 billion, or 19.6% higher than last year's $6.75 billion through Oct. 11, according to Rentrak. The domestic box office crossed the $8 billion mark on Friday, as projected, 59 days earlier than in 2025. With this year's record summer movie season of $4.77 billion, and the holiday moviegoing season still to come, Dergarabedian sees the potential to hit $9 billion in annual ticket sales.

The horror genre has helped play a part in that. "Horror movies have generated approximately $1.28 billion domestically this year," already 90% of last year's record $1.426 billion and "roughly $150 million away from another record, with 81 days remaining in 2026," Dergarabedian said.

Upcoming horror films include: Crawlers (opening Oct. 16), Clayface (Oct. 23), Christmas at the Kringles (Oct. 30), Victorian Psycho (Nov. 13), and Werwulf (Dec. 25), making another record-breaking year for the horror genre "a very real possibility," he said.

Eric Handler, Roth senior media and entertainment analyst, said the third-quarter North American box office finished at a record high of $3.049 billion, nearly 29% from a year ago and above the previous $2.98 billion record set in 2016. Of that total, 52% of the revenue came from two movies: Spider-Man: Brand New Day with $952 million, and The Odyssey at $619 million.

Domestic box office is on pace to finish at "a post-pandemic high of almost $10.3 billion," up 19% from 2025, he wrote. Handler projects fourth-quarter domestic box office of $2.525 billion, or 16% higher than 2025, with the quarter "heavily weighted towards December," because of the releases of Avengers: Doomsday, Dune: Part Three, and Jumanji: Open World, all opening on Dec. 18. They are collectively expected to surpass $1 billion in box office revenue.

This weekend, Amazon MGM's Verity, an R-rated psychological thriller starring Anne Hathaway, Dakota Johnson, and Josh Hartnett, took second place at the domestic box office with an estimated $11.5 million in ticket sales in its second weekend, bringing its domestic total to $53.9 million and its worldwide total to $113.8 million, according to Rentrak.

Sony's Columbia Pictures' Resident Evil, a horror movie about a hapless courier fighting mutant creatures to deliver a package to a remote hospital, sold nearly $8.4 million in its fourth weekend, bringing its domestic total to $138.5 million. The movie, directed by Zach Cregger and starring Austin Abrams, was the No. 1 movie worldwide this weekend, with $62.7 million in ticket sales, bringing its global total to $320.2 million, including a record $40.6 million opening in China. The movie is based on a popular videogame franchise.

Sony Pictures' The Social Reckoning, the biographic thriller about Facebook engineer Frances Haugen divulging the social network's most guarded secrets with the help of then-Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz, opened with an underwhelming $5.5 million domestically and $9 million worldwide. The movie opens in Brazil and Mexico on Oct. 22.

"The Social Reckoning is a very high-profile film written and directed by Aaron Sorkin, but it's also a prestige picture that appeals to a very different audience than a mainstream blockbuster or genre film," Dergarabedian said.

"Horror is a genre where audiences just want to go out and have fun at the movie theater, so it's not surprising that a Blumhouse horror movie like Other Mommy would have a much bigger opening weekend than a prestige picture like The Social Reckoning." He noted that The Social Network, which was a big hit when it opened in 2010, was a bigger-budgeted film and a different type of movie.

The Social Reckoning came in fifth place this weekend, after Paramount Pictures' Heart of the Beast, an action adventure starring Brad Pitt as a Special Forces veteran fighting to survive in the Alaskan wilderness with his combat dog. Heart of the Beast sold an estimated $7.1 million in its third weekend, bringing its domestic total to $49.7 million and its global total to $131.4 million.

"We're in awards season, and that means we're going to have high-profile films from great filmmakers that are potential Oscar contenders," but aren't necessarily going to generate massive box office numbers when they debut, he said. "The bigger test for these films is how they hold up in weekend two and weekend three," and whether they can build their audiences through word of mouth.

Warner Bros.' Digger, a dark comedy starring Tom Cruise and made for about $125 million, sold only $9.6 million of tickets in its second weekend, bringing its domestic total to $14.4 million and its global take to $35.3 million.

Bleecker Street's Musk, a nearly four-hour long documentary about the rise, influence, and power of Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, sold an estimated $68,900 from only four theaters its opening weekend. Featuring Elon Musk in archival footage and directed by Alex Gibney, who directed the 2005 documentary Enron: The Smartest Guys in the Room, the Musk film opens more widely this month.
